title: My Friend, Covered with Golden Light
lead: A song about the mystical awakening of the soul and meeting the Supreme as an eternal, close Friend. The central image is the dawn bird of the heart spreading new wings in the golden radiance of illumination.

lines.structure: Repeated poetic address with possessive pronoun: [O] my Friend, my Friend.
lines.image_note: Addressing the Supreme principle as the closest and most intimate Friend (Bandhu).

lines.structure: Nominal sentence: [You are] covered (predicate dháká) with golden light (adverbial/object sonár áloy).
lines.image_note: The golden light of dawn symbolizes divine illumination and the awakening of consciousness.
Conclusion of the first stanza and affirmation of the personal bond.

words.form: sing., gen. case with poetic extension (-era/-ere)
words.note: In the text Bhorera (sung bhorere) - poetic vocalization of the suffix -er.

words.meaning_here: set to, began to sing (as part of compound verb)

words.note: Construction d́ákii ut́hlo (compound verb denoting sudden onset of action: burst into song, cried out).

lines.structure: Subject - bhorera pákhii (bird of dawn), compound verbal predicate - d́ákii ut́hlo (burst into song, started to call).
lines.literal: Of morning the bird rose calling,
lines.natural: The bird of dawn begins to sing,
lines.image_note: The image of a bird singing at dawn conveys the soul's thrilling awakening from a long slumber.

words.meaning_here: of life force, of breath of life

lines.structure: Attributive phrase modifying 'bird' (pákhii): [all] dusted (mákhá) with life's pollen (práńer parág).
lines.natural: Vibrant with the pollen of life,
lines.image_note: «Pollen of life» - an image of freshness, vitality, and spiritual renewal, like the nectar of a blossomed flower.
Return to the image of the Beloved after the scene of dawn.

words.meaning_here: to the call, by the call

lines.structure: A series of coordinate interrogative adverbials: for what sake (kiser tare), in answer to what call (kiser d́áke).
lines.natural: Why all this? In answer to whose call,
lines.image_note: Bewilderment and wonder of the seeking mind before the soul's irresistible pull toward the Infinite.

words.note: The nasal sound candrabindu is pronounced as slight nasalization or similar to 'n'.

lines.structure: Main clause: Subject [I] is implied; predicate - khuṊji (I seek); object - táke (Him); adverbials - dine ráte (day and night).
lines.literal: by day [and] by night seek [I] Him?
lines.natural: Day and night, do I seek Him?
lines.image_note: Unceasing inner search, independent of the external schedule of the day.

words.note: From Sanskr. nūtana (new). Spelling with 'o' reflects pronunciation.

words.meaning_here: emits, gives (jhalkáni dey = flashes forth, shines)

lines.structure: Compound predicate jhalkáni dey (gives a flash / blazes forth), adverbial - notun áloy (in new light). Subject is implied ("He" or "dawn").
lines.natural: The new light sends forth a blaze of effulgence,
lines.image_note: Sudden burst of mystical light illuminating the entire consciousness.

words.form: plur. (in collective sing. form), dir. case

lines.structure: Predicate - doláy (flaps / sways); direct object - notun pákhá (new wings). Subject - the bird of the soul (pákhii).
lines.natural: And beats its new wings of joy,
lines.image_note: «New wings» - symbol of acquiring a new spiritual capacity to fly toward the Infinite.
Final return to the contemplation of the Supreme Friend.

heard: In line 0, the refrain is performed with a twofold repetition of the phrase: 'Bandhu a'ma'r, bandhu a'ma'r'.
In line 3, the poetic extension of the genitive case ending is clearly heard: 'Bhorere pakhii' instead of the strict literary 'Bhorer'.
In the stanzas, the lines are sung with repetition of half-lines before transitioning to the refrain.
interpretation: The song expresses an ecstatic state of the awakening of the soul (samádhi/enlightenment or the state after initiation). The Supreme Entity appears not as a stern master, but as the closest, most intimate Friend (Bandhu), enveloped in the golden light of supreme love. The soul is likened to a bird of dawn which, having cast off the shackles of ignorance, becomes dusted with the blessed «pollen of life» and spreads radiant wings for an endless flight across the ocean of divine joy.
